result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.dominance_frontiers()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the dominance frontier of every node reachable from a start node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L45620-L45688){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.dominance_frontiers(start) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Dominance frontiers](/assets/graphs/dominance-frontiers.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same if/else control-flow graph from entry. The branches then and else are outlined: each dominates only itself, and its edge into merge (accent) leaves its region, so merge, filled in accent, is the dominance frontier of both. The card lists every node's frontier: merge for then and else, and empty for the others." width="100%"} The dominance frontier of a node `d` is the set of nodes where `d`'s dominance ends: the nodes `v` that `d` does not strictly dominate, but that have a predecessor dominated by `d` (see `immediate_dominators()`). They are the merge points where paths from inside and outside `d`'s region meet. Compilers use them to place phi functions when building static single assignment form; in other networks they mark where the influence of an unavoidable node stops being exclusive. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [start]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The start (entry) node, as an ID or label. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, set[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : For every node ID reachable from `start`, the set of node IDs in its frontier. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected or `start` does not exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Following Cooper, Harvey and Kennedy (2001), as in NetworkX: for every join node `v` (two or more predecessors), each reachable predecessor walks up the dominator tree until reaching `v`'s immediate dominator, adding `v` to the frontier of every node passed. The cost is proportional to the total size of the frontiers after computing the dominators. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In an if/else, the frontier of each branch is the merge node where the branches rejoin: ::: {#1bc631eb .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["entry", "if", "then", "else", "merge", "exit"]) g.add_edges( [ ("entry", "if"), ("if", "then"), ("if", "else"), ("then", "merge"), ("else", "merge"), ("merge", "exit"), ] ) frontiers = g.dominance_frontiers("entry") {g.get_label_from_id(n): sorted(g.get_label_from_id(f) for f in fs) for n, fs in frontiers.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'entry': [], 'if': [], 'then': ['merge'], 'else': ['merge'], 'merge': [], 'exit': []} ``` ::: :::
